The asymmetry that matters: a recall failure is unrecoverable. If the answer isn't in what you retrieved, nothing downstream can produce it — not a better prompt, not a bigger model, not reranking. The information simply isn't in the context.

A precision failure is recoverable. Noisy results can be reranked and filtered.

So the stages have different jobs: retrieval maximises recall, reranking then maximises precision.
more: This gives you a clean debugging procedure. Measure recall@50 on your evaluation set first. Poor recall means fixing chunking, embeddings or hybrid search — the prompt is irrelevant. Good recall with poor answers means the information was there and something later mishandled it: reranking, ordering, or the prompt itself. Two very different afternoons of work.
diagram2:
Retrieval stage  → maximise recall@50
  "is the answer anywhere in these 50?"
  miss here → nothing downstream can help ✗

Rerank stage     → maximise precision@3
  "are these 3 the best of the 50?"
  noise here → fixable ✓

Debug order:
  recall@50 low?  → chunking / embeddings / hybrid
  recall fine?    → reranking / ordering / prompt

means: Merging ranked lists using rank position rather than raw scores, so you don't have to normalise incomparable scoring scales.
example: BM25 scores range 0-40 and cosine 0-1. Normalising them is fragile; RRF just uses positions and works well with almost no tuning.
diagram:
score(d) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_i(d)),  k ≈ 60

dense rank 3, sparse rank 1
  → 1/63 + 1/61

No score normalisation needed
how:
When you run two retrievers you get two ranked lists, and you need one. The obvious approach — add the scores — doesn't work, because the scores aren't on the same scale. BM25 might return 0 to 40 with no fixed ceiling; cosine returns roughly -1 to 1. Adding them lets whichever has larger numbers dominate.

You could normalise, but normalisation is fragile: it depends on the score range in this particular result set, so it shifts from query to query.

RRF sidesteps the problem by throwing away the scores entirely and using only positions. A document's contribution from each list is one divided by a constant plus its rank. Being first is worth a lot, being twentieth is worth little, and how confident the retriever claimed to be is irrelevant.

Documents ranked well by both lists rise to the top.
more: Its main virtue is that it works well immediately with essentially no tuning, which is rare. The constant (conventionally around 60) softens the difference between the top few positions so a single retriever's first result doesn't automatically win. If you later need to favour one retriever, add a weight per list rather than reaching back for score normalisation.
diagram2:
score(doc) = Σ over lists of  1 / (60 + rank)

doc X: dense rank 1, sparse rank 40
  → 1/61 + 1/100 = 0.0264
doc Y: dense rank 3, sparse rank 2
  → 1/63 + 1/62 = 0.0320  ← wins ✓

Good in both beats excellent in one.
No score normalisation needed at all.

means: A second, more expensive model that scores query-document pairs jointly and reorders the candidate set. Usually the single biggest RAG quality win.
example: Vector search returns 50 candidates in 10ms. A cross-encoder reranks them in 80ms and the top 3 are far more relevant. Answer quality jumps visibly.
diagram:
query → vector search → 50 candidates (fast, approximate)
      → cross-encoder rerank (accurate, slower)
      → top 3 into the prompt

Bi-encoder: separate embeddings, fast
Cross-encoder: reads both together, accurate
how:
Retrieval and reranking use two different kinds of model, and the difference explains why the two-stage design exists.

The embedding model used for retrieval is a bi-encoder: it turns the query into a vector and each document into a vector, separately, and compares them. Because documents are embedded ahead of time, search is fast — but the model never sees the query and document together, so it can only compare summaries of each.

A reranker is a cross-encoder: it reads the query and one document *at the same time* and scores how well that document answers that query. Far more accurate, and far more expensive, because nothing can be precomputed — it's a full model pass per pair.

So you use each where it fits: the bi-encoder searches millions fast, the cross-encoder carefully ranks the fifty it returned.
more: This is reliably one of the highest-return additions to a RAG pipeline, for two compounding reasons. Quality improves because the top results are genuinely more relevant. And because they're better, you can send fewer chunks to the model — which cuts cost, cuts prefill latency, and sidesteps the lost-in-the-middle problem all at once.
diagram2:
BI-ENCODER (retrieval)
  query → vector ┐
  doc   → vector ┘ compare vectors
  precomputed, milliseconds, millions of docs

CROSS-ENCODER (rerank)
  [query + doc] → model → relevance score
  reads both together, ~80ms for 50 pairs

search 10M → 50 candidates → rerank → top 3 ✓
  cheap and broad      accurate and narrow

means: Question-to-document pairs that let you measure retrieval independently of generation. Otherwise you tune prompts to fix a retrieval bug.
example: Answer quality was poor. The eval set showed recall@10 was 61% — the model was fine, retrieval was starving it.
diagram:
100 questions → known correct chunk IDs
  ↓ measure recall@k, MRR, nDCG
  ↓ retrieval broken? fix retrieval
  ↓ retrieval fine but answers bad? fix generation

Debug the stages separately
how:
RAG has two stages that fail independently, and a single end-to-end quality score can't tell you which one broke.

A retrieval evaluation set isolates the first stage. It's a list of questions, each paired with the chunk IDs that genuinely contain the answer — determined by a human reading the corpus, not by what your current system returns.

With it you can measure retrieval on its own terms: recall@k, mean reciprocal rank, nDCG. These are answerable without calling a generation model at all, which makes them fast, cheap and deterministic — you can run them on every ingest change.

The payoff is that you stop guessing. "Answers are bad" becomes "recall@10 is 61%", which is a specific problem with specific fixes, none of which involve the prompt.
more: Build it from real user questions rather than invented ones, and deliberately include questions your corpus cannot answer — the correct retrieval behaviour there is returning nothing above threshold, and a system that always returns its best five chunks regardless will fail that case while scoring well on everything else.
diagram2:
100 real questions → correct chunk IDs
  (a human read the corpus and decided)

measure without any model call:
  recall@10  did we find it at all?
  MRR        how high did it rank?
  nDCG       is the ordering sensible?

recall@10 = 61%
  → retrieval problem. The prompt is irrelevant.

Include unanswerable questions:
  correct behaviour is returning nothing.

means: The cycle of model → tool call → observation → model, repeating until done. Everything called an 'agent' is some version of this loop.
example: Without a step cap and a cost cap, a confused agent loops on a failing tool 400 times and burns the daily budget in an afternoon.
diagram:
think → act (tool) → observe → repeat
  ↑____________________________|

Guardrails: max steps, max cost, max wall time,
loop detection, human approval for risky actions
how:
An agent is a loop, and the loop is short: the model receives context and decides either to answer or to call a tool. If it calls a tool, your code runs it and feeds the result back. Repeat.

Everything marketed as agentic is some version of this. The intelligence is in the model's choice at each step; the engineering is entirely in the control structure around it.

Which is where it goes wrong. The model has no reliable sense of how long it has been going or how much it has spent. A tool that returns an unhelpful error can be retried indefinitely, each attempt looking locally reasonable, with the whole run making no progress.

Without external limits, a confused agent will keep going until something else stops it — usually a bill or a timeout.
more: Cap steps, total tokens, wall-clock time and spend, per run. Add loop detection: if the same tool is called with the same arguments three times, stop rather than continue. And when a cap trips, surface the partial result and an alert instead of failing silently — a truncated answer with an explanation is far more useful than a spinner that never resolves.
diagram2:
┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │  model decides              │
  │    ├ answer → done          │
  │    └ call tool              │
  │         ↓                   │
  │  your code executes         │
  │         ↓                   │
  │  result back into context ──┘

Required caps per run:
  max steps · max tokens · max wall time
  max spend · repeated-call detection

Cap tripped → partial result + alert,
              never a silent hang.

means: Tracing every prompt, tool call, observation and token cost per run. Without it, 'the agent did something weird' is unfixable.
example: A trace showed the agent retried a tool 12 times because a 400 error was returned as a plain string the model read as 'try again'.
diagram:
per run: full prompt, each tool call + result,
  tokens, latency, cost, final output
   ↓
replayable, diffable, comparable across prompts

LangSmith / Langfuse / OTel GenAI conventions
how:
When an agent misbehaves, the report you get is "it did something weird". Without a record you cannot investigate, because the run is gone — and re-running it may produce different behaviour.

What you need captured is everything that determined the outcome: the fully rendered prompt at each step, every tool call with its arguments, every result returned, the model and version, tokens and cost per step, and the final output.

The rendered prompt is the part teams skip and need most. Your code assembles it from templates, retrieved context and history, so the template alone doesn't tell you what the model actually saw. Most surprising agent behaviour turns out to be a prompt that assembled differently than expected.

With a complete trace, debugging is reading. Without one, it's guessing.
more: Trace data is also your evaluation dataset. Real runs with real inputs and known-bad outcomes are exactly the cases a regression suite should contain, and they're better than anything you'd invent. Capture with sampling on the happy path to control cost, and keep everything for failures and anomalies.
diagram2:
Per run, capture:
  ├ rendered prompt at each step  ← most skipped
  ├ every tool call + arguments
  ├ every result returned
  ├ model + version, tokens, cost, latency
  └ final output + termination reason

"It did something weird"
  no trace  → unreproducible, unfixable
  trace     → read it, find the assembled prompt

Failed runs become regression cases.

means: Deciding what enters the context window and in what order. At long context lengths this matters more than prompt wording.
example: Cutting from 40 retrieved chunks to the 6 best, with the most relevant first, improved accuracy and cut cost 70% at once.
diagram:
Budget the window deliberately:
  system + tools     stable, cached
  retrieved context  fewer, reranked, best first
  history            summarise or truncate old turns
  output reserve     don't get truncated mid-answer
how:
Prompt engineering is about wording. Context engineering is about what goes into the window at all, and in what order — and at long context lengths it matters considerably more.

The window is a fixed budget shared by everything: system prompt, tool definitions, conversation history, retrieved documents, and the space reserved for the answer. Every token spent on one is unavailable to the others.

Two forces push against just filling it. Cost scales directly with input tokens. And attention is uneven — material buried in the middle of a long context gets missed measurably more often than material at the start or end.

So the discipline is subtractive. Fewer, better-chosen chunks, placed deliberately, beat more chunks almost every time.
more: A practical layout that works: stable content first so it caches, the strongest retrieved material immediately after, conversation history summarised rather than verbatim once it gets long, and the user's actual question last so it sits at the end where attention is reliable. Then reserve output space explicitly — running out mid-answer is a bad failure that looks like a model problem.
diagram2:
Budget the window deliberately:

[ system + tools ]  stable → cached
[ retrieved: 5 reranked, best first ]
[ history: summarised beyond ~20 turns ]
[ user question ]   last → end position ✓
[ reserved for output ]

40 chunks → 6 reranked chunks
  cost −70%, accuracy UP
  (fewer near-misses to get lost among)

means: Requiring approval before consequential actions. The difference between a useful agent and an incident report.
example: Read-only tools run freely; anything that sends email, moves money or deletes data requires explicit confirmation showing the exact action.
diagram:
read-only tools    → auto-execute ✓
write/irreversible → show the exact action,
                     require approval ✓

Approval UI must show what will happen,
not just "the agent wants to continue".
how:
The design question for any agent is not how autonomous it can be, but which actions require a human to say yes.

The useful line is reversibility. Reading data, searching, drafting — all reversible, all fine to run automatically. Sending an email, moving money, deleting records, posting publicly — none of those can be undone, and each should require explicit confirmation.

The approval interface matters as much as the policy. "The agent wants to continue" gives the human nothing to evaluate, and people click through it within a day. Showing the concrete action — this exact recipient, this exact amount, this exact record — is what makes review real rather than ceremonial.

An approval step people rubber-stamp is worse than none, because it manufactures the appearance of oversight.
more: Approval fatigue is the failure mode to design against. If every trivial action prompts, users stop reading. Scope approvals to what's genuinely consequential, allow standing approvals for low-risk repeated actions, and batch related actions into a single review. The goal is a small number of decisions people actually think about.
diagram2:
AUTO — reversible
  read · search · summarise · draft

APPROVE — irreversible or external
  send · pay · delete · publish · escalate

Bad approval prompt:
  "The agent wants to continue"   → rubber-stamped

Good approval prompt:
  "Send this email to 1,240 customers:
   Subject: ...  Body: ...      [Approve] [Edit]"

Too many prompts → nobody reads any of them.

means: Agents retry. A tool without idempotency turns one retry into two emails, two refunds or two tickets.
example: `send_email` called twice because the model didn't see the first result sends two emails. Accepting a dedup key makes the second call a no-op.
diagram:
agent retries (it will)
  send_email() twice → 2 emails ✗
  send_email(idempotency_key) → 1 email ✓

Same rule as any distributed consumer
how:
Agents retry. The model may not see a tool result, may decide the first attempt failed, or may simply call the same thing twice while working through a problem. This is normal behaviour, not a bug to eliminate.

Which means any tool with a side effect will eventually be invoked twice for one intent. If `send_email` isn't idempotent, that's two emails. If `create_refund` isn't, that's two refunds.

The fix is the same as for any distributed consumer: accept a key identifying the intent, record it with the result, and on a repeat return the stored result without redoing the work.

The key must identify the *intent*, not the call. Generated per attempt, it defeats the purpose entirely — every retry gets a fresh key and executes again.
more: Where a natural key exists, use it — an order ID for a refund, a message ID for a send. Where none does, derive one deterministically from the arguments so identical calls collapse. And return a clear signal on the duplicate path, so the agent's trace shows a deduplicated repeat rather than looking like two successes.
diagram2:
agent calls send_email(...)
  → sent, but the agent doesn't see the result
agent calls send_email(...) again
  → two emails ✗

With an intent key:
  key seen?  no  → send, store (key → result)
             yes → return stored result, no send ✓

Key must identify the INTENT:
  ✓ "refund:order-91"
  ✗ uuid4() generated per attempt

means: Short-term memory is the conversation in context; long-term memory is retrieved from a store. Conflating them produces agents that forget or drown.
example: Storing every message forever and injecting all of it fills the window with noise. Summarising older turns and retrieving only relevant facts scales.
diagram:
Short-term: recent turns in context (bounded)
Long-term:  facts in a store, retrieved on demand

Strategy: summarise old turns,
extract durable facts, retrieve by relevance
how:
"Memory" covers two unrelated mechanisms, and conflating them causes most memory bugs.

Short-term memory is the conversation currently in the context window. It's not stored anywhere — your application resends it each turn. It's complete and exact, and it's bounded by the window.

Long-term memory is facts persisted in a database and retrieved when relevant. It survives across sessions and can hold far more than fits in a window, but only what you retrieve is available on any given turn.

The naive approach — store every message and inject all of it — fails at both ends. It overflows the window and it fills the context with irrelevant history that crowds out what matters.

Working systems summarise old turns for the short term and store *extracted facts*, not transcripts, for the long term.
more: Deciding what's worth remembering is the hard part, and it's a product question more than a technical one. Durable preferences and stable facts belong in long-term memory. Transient state from one task does not. Getting this wrong is uncomfortable in a specific way: an assistant confidently applying something the user mentioned once, months ago, in a different context, feels worse than one that simply forgot.
diagram2:
SHORT-TERM — the context window
  resent every turn, exact, bounded
  beyond ~20 turns → summarise the old ones

LONG-TERM — a store you retrieve from
  survives sessions, unbounded
  only what you retrieve is available

Store extracted FACTS, not transcripts:
  ✓ "prefers metric units"
  ✗ the 40-message conversation where they said it

Wrong call here reads as creepy, not helpful.

means: Splitting work across specialised agents. Real benefits for parallelisable work, and real cost in latency, tokens and debuggability.
example: Three agents debating a simple question is slower, pricier and worse than one good prompt. Fanning out ten independent document reviews is a genuine win.
diagram:
Good: parallel independent subtasks,
      genuinely different tool sets
Bad:  "agents discussing" a simple task

Every hop adds latency, tokens, failure modes
how:
Splitting work across several specialised agents is appealing and frequently the wrong choice, so it's worth being precise about when it helps.

It genuinely helps when subtasks are independent and can run in parallel — reviewing forty documents, or gathering from several sources at once. Wall-clock time drops because the work is actually concurrent. It also helps when subtasks need genuinely different tools and permissions, so isolation is a security property.

It doesn't help when agents "discuss" a problem. Each hop adds latency, tokens and another chance to lose information in a handoff. A single well-prompted call is usually faster, cheaper and better.

The costs compound in a way that's easy to underestimate: three agents is three times the failure modes and a debugging story where you must reconstruct who told whom what.
more: If you do split, keep handoffs explicit and structured — a defined schema passed between agents, not free-form prose that the next agent reinterprets. And trace the whole run under one identifier, or you'll be correlating separate logs by timestamp during an incident, which is exactly when you can least afford it.
diagram2:
WORTH IT — genuinely parallel
  40 documents → 40 concurrent reviews
  wall-clock time actually drops ✓

WORTH IT — different tool sets
  one agent can write, one can only read
  isolation is a security property ✓

NOT WORTH IT — "agents discussing"
  3x latency, 3x tokens, 3x failure modes
  a single good prompt usually wins ✗

Structured handoffs. One trace ID for the run.

means: Interleaving reasoning and acting: the model states why it's calling a tool, calls it, then reasons about the result. The reasoning trace makes debugging possible.
example: The trace shows the agent searched the wrong field name three times. Without the reasoning steps you'd only see three failed tool calls and no reason.
diagram:
Thought: I need the order status
Action: get_order(id=91)
Observation: {status: "shipped"}
Thought: now I can answer
Answer: ...
how:
ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting: before each tool call the model states why it's making it, then makes it, then reasons about what came back.

The practical value isn't that the model performs better — it's that the run becomes legible. Without the reasoning steps, a failed agent run is a list of tool calls with no explanation, and you're left inferring intent from arguments.

With them, you can see the mistake. "I need the customer's order history, so I'll search by email" followed by an empty result tells you immediately that the agent had the wrong lookup key — not that the tool was broken, not that the model was confused, but one specific incorrect assumption.

That difference turns agent debugging from archaeology into reading.
more: The reasoning text also gives you something to evaluate. You can score whether the agent's stated plan was sensible separately from whether the outcome was correct, which distinguishes "good plan, broken tool" from "the tools worked and the plan was wrong". Those need completely different fixes and look identical from the outcome alone.
diagram2:
Thought: I need this customer's orders.
         I have their email, so I'll search by email.
Action:  search_orders(email="a@b.com")
Observation: []
Thought: Empty. Perhaps orders are keyed by
         customer_id, not email. Let me look that up.
Action:  get_customer(email="a@b.com")

Without the Thought lines:
  two tool calls, one empty result, no reason.

Evaluate plan quality and outcome separately.

means: Tool names, descriptions and parameter docs are prompt engineering. Bad descriptions cause wrong tool selection more often than model weakness does.
example: Renaming `search()` to `search_internal_docs()` and describing exactly when not to use it cut wrong-tool selection from 22% to 4%.
diagram:
Bad:  search(q) — "searches"
Good: search_internal_docs(query, doc_type)
  "Search company policy documents.
   Use for internal policy questions.
   Do NOT use for customer data — use get_customer."

Fewer, clearer tools > many overlapping ones
how:
The model chooses tools based on nothing but their names, descriptions and parameter documentation. That text is the entire basis of the decision — so it's prompt engineering, not API documentation.

Most wrong-tool selection traces back to this rather than to model capability. A tool called `search` with the description "searches" gives the model nothing to distinguish it from three other search-like tools. It will guess, and it will guess inconsistently.

Descriptions should say what the tool does, when to use it, and — this is the part usually missing — when *not* to. An explicit "do not use this for customer data; use get_customer instead" resolves ambiguity far more effectively than describing the correct tool more thoroughly.

Parameter descriptions matter equally. "date" invites any format; "date in YYYY-MM-DD format, e.g. 2026-03-14" gets one.
more: Tool count matters too. Beyond roughly fifteen or twenty, selection accuracy degrades — the model is choosing from a long list of partially overlapping options. Consolidating similar tools, or splitting the agent so each has a smaller focused set, usually works better than continuing to refine descriptions.
diagram2:
Poor:
  search(q)  "searches"

Good:
  search_policy_docs(query, doc_type)
  "Search internal HR and IT policy documents.
   Use for questions about company policy.
   Do NOT use for customer records — use
   get_customer. Do NOT use for live system
   status — use check_status."

Wrong-tool rate: 22% → 4%
Beyond ~20 tools, selection degrades regardless.

means: Coordinates for every recognised token, so you can extract by position and highlight the source in the UI.
example: The invoice total is 'the number to the right of the word Total'. Bounding boxes make that rule expressible; a flat text dump doesn't.
diagram:
token "Total"  bbox [412, 890, 468, 908]
token "₹4,500" bbox [520, 890, 590, 908]
   ↓ same y, x to the right → the total ✓
   ↓ also powers click-to-source highlighting
how:
Good OCR returns each recognised token with its coordinates on the page — the rectangle it occupies. Discarding those and keeping only the text throws away the document's structure.

Position is what makes rule-based extraction possible. "The total is the number to the right of the word Total" is a precise instruction with coordinates and impossible without them. So is "the invoice number is in the top-right quadrant" and "these values belong to the same row because their vertical centres align".

Coordinates also power the interface feature that makes document AI trustworthy: click an extracted value and the source region highlights on the page image. A human verifies in one second instead of reading the document.

That review speed is often what determines whether the system is usable at scale.
more: Keep coordinates normalised relative to page dimensions rather than in absolute pixels, so the same rules work across resolutions and page sizes. And store the page number with them — a rule that finds the right region on the wrong page is a subtle bug that surfaces only on multi-page documents.
diagram2:
token "Total"    bbox [412, 890, 468, 908]
token "₹4,500"   bbox [520, 890, 590, 908]
                        ↑ same vertical band,
                          immediately to the right
→ that is the total ✓

Impossible from a flat text dump.

Also enables click-to-source highlighting:
  human verifies in 1 second, not 1 minute
  → often decides whether review scales

Normalise coordinates. Store the page number.

means: Deciding what kind of document arrived before extracting from it, so the right pipeline runs.
example: A pipeline expecting invoices received a delivery note and extracted garbage confidently. A classification gate routes it correctly or rejects it.
diagram:
incoming doc → classifier
  invoice   → invoice extractor
  contract  → clause extractor
  unknown   → human queue ✓

Never assume every input matches your happy path
how:
A pipeline built for invoices, handed a delivery note, will extract from it confidently and produce nonsense. Nothing errors — the extractor finds something that looks like a total and returns it.

Classification is the gate that prevents this. Before extraction, decide what kind of document this is and route accordingly.

The part teams get wrong is the unknown case. A classifier forced to choose among invoice, contract and receipt will pick the nearest one for a document that is none of them. It needs an explicit "unrecognised" outcome that routes to a human, and a confidence threshold below which nothing is assumed.

Getting this right early is disproportionately valuable, because every downstream error caused by a misrouted document is expensive to trace back — the extraction looks like the failure, and the real cause is two steps upstream.
more: Classification is often possible from cheap signals before any full recognition: page count, presence of certain keywords in the first region, aspect ratio, whether it's scanned or digitally generated. Running the cheap check first and only invoking the expensive model on ambiguous cases keeps the gate from becoming the bottleneck.
diagram2:
incoming document
  ↓ classifier
  ├ invoice     → invoice extractor
  ├ contract    → clause extractor
  ├ receipt     → receipt extractor
  └ unknown / low confidence → human queue ✓
                               ↑ the part usually missing

Without the unknown branch:
  a delivery note gets invoice-extracted
  → confident, structured, wrong
  → and the bug looks like an extraction bug

means: Hand-labelled documents used to measure field-level accuracy. Without it, 'the OCR is good' is an opinion.
example: A 200-document labelled set showed total amount at 97% and vendor address at 71%. Effort went where the number was actually bad.
diagram:
200 docs, every field hand-labelled
  ↓ measure per field, not overall
  invoice_number  99%
  total_amount    97%
  vendor_address  71%  ← fix this one
how:
"The OCR is good" is an opinion until you have documents where a human has recorded the correct value for every field, and you can measure against them.

The measurement that matters is per field, not overall. An aggregate accuracy of 94% is nearly useless information — it averages the fields that work with the ones that don't, and hides which is which.

Broken out, the picture is usually lopsided and immediately actionable: invoice number at 99%, total at 97%, supplier address at 71%. Now you know exactly where the remaining effort goes, and that most of the pipeline is fine.

Building the set is genuine manual work — a couple of hundred documents, every field labelled by hand — and it's the work that makes every subsequent decision measurable rather than argued.
more: Sample it to match reality, not convenience. If a fifth of production input is phone photographs, a fifth of the ground truth set should be too. A set built from clean digital PDFs will report excellent accuracy and predict nothing about the documents your users actually send.
diagram2:
200 documents, every field labelled by hand

Aggregate: 94%   ← tells you nothing

Per field:
  invoice_number   99%  ✓
  total_amount     97%  ✓
  line_items       89%
  supplier_address 71%  ← all the effort goes here

Sample to match production:
  20% phone photos in reality
  → 20% phone photos in the set

means: Routing low-confidence extractions to people, and feeding their corrections back as training data.
example: 15% of documents route to review. Corrections become labelled examples, and the review rate falls over time as the model improves on real failures.
diagram:
extraction
  ├ high confidence → auto-approve (85%)
  └ low confidence  → review queue (15%)
                        ↓ corrections
                     training data → fewer reviews
how:
No extraction pipeline reaches 100%, so the question isn't whether humans are involved but how efficiently.

A review queue routes low-confidence or validation-failing extractions to people, while everything else passes automatically. That single split is what makes the economics work — if 85% auto-processes, human effort applies to the remaining 15% rather than to everything.

The design detail that determines throughput is what the reviewer sees. Presenting a form of extracted values requires them to read the whole document to verify. Presenting the values with each one highlighted on the page image lets them confirm at a glance.

The difference is roughly an order of magnitude in review time, which is usually the difference between the queue keeping up and the queue growing.
more: Corrections are training data, and capturing them closes the loop: today's review population becomes tomorrow's improvement, and the review rate declines over time. Track that rate as a headline metric — if it isn't falling, the loop isn't actually connected, and you've built a permanent manual process wearing an automation label.
diagram2:
extraction
  ├ high confidence + validations pass → auto (85%)
  └ low confidence or failed validation → queue (15%)

Reviewer interface decides throughput:
  form of values only
    → must read the whole document  ~60s/doc
  values + highlighted source regions
    → confirm at a glance             ~6s/doc

corrections → labelled data → fewer reviews

If the review rate isn't falling,
the feedback loop isn't connected.

means: Turning recognised text into structured fields. Template rules are exact and brittle; models generalise and hallucinate.
example: Template rules handled 6 known invoice vendors perfectly and failed on the 7th. An LLM handled all of them at 94% and occasionally invented a field.
diagram:
Template/regex: exact, brittle, per-vendor
Layout model:   generalises, needs training data
LLM on OCR text: flexible, can hallucinate
   ↓
Hybrid: LLM extract + validate against
        the OCR tokens actually present
how:
OCR gives you text. What you actually need is structured fields — invoice number, date, total — and getting from one to the other is its own problem.

Three approaches, with different failure characteristics.

Template rules match known layouts by position or regex. Exact and fast for a vendor you've configured, completely broken for a vendor you haven't. They scale linearly with the number of vendors, which stops working somewhere around a few dozen.

Layout models learn the visual relationship between labels and values, so they generalise to unseen layouts. They need training data.

An LLM over the OCR text handles arbitrary formats with no per-vendor work, and will occasionally invent a value that was never on the page.

That last failure mode is the one that determines the design.
more: The hybrid that works in practice: extract with a model, then verify every returned value actually appears among the OCR tokens, and check arithmetic where it exists — line items should sum to the total. That single validation step catches most fabrication, and turns "confidently wrong" into "flagged for review", which is a completely different operational problem.
diagram2:
Template rules   exact · brittle · per-vendor
Layout model     generalises · needs training data
LLM on OCR text  flexible · can invent values ✗

Hybrid that works:

  LLM extracts {"total": "4,500"}
    ↓ verify: does "4,500" exist in OCR tokens?
    ↓ verify: do line items sum to 4,500?
    ↓ fail either → route to review ✓

Turns silent fabrication into a flagged case.

means: Detecting the structure — columns, tables, headers, reading order — before extracting text. Skipping it scrambles multi-column documents.
example: A two-column contract read without layout analysis interleaves the columns line by line, producing text that is grammatically nonsense.
diagram:
raw OCR (no layout):
  "Term 1 ... Term 8 ... shall not ... liability"
   ↑ columns interleaved ✗

with layout: regions detected → correct reading order ✓
how:
Before recognising any characters, the system has to work out the geometry of the page: where the text blocks are, which are columns, what's a table, what's a header, and crucially what order a human would read them in.

Skip it and OCR reads strictly left to right across the full page width. On a two-column contract that interleaves the columns line by line, producing text that is grammatically incoherent — the words are all correct and the meaning is destroyed.

This failure is nastier than a recognition error because nothing looks wrong at the character level. Confidence scores are high. The text is real. It's just in an order that means nothing, and every downstream step inherits the damage.

Layout analysis segments the page into regions first, then recognises each region separately and reassembles in reading order.
more: It also supplies the structure downstream steps depend on. Knowing a region is a table means you can extract rows and columns rather than a stream of numbers. Knowing a line is a heading means you can chunk on it for retrieval. Layout is where a document stops being a picture of text and becomes a document.
diagram2:
Two-column page, no layout analysis:

  "Term 1. The parties  Term 8. Liability
   agree that...        shall not exceed..."
  read left-to-right across BOTH columns
  → "Term 1. The parties Term 8. Liability"
  → grammatically meaningless ✗

High confidence. Real words. Useless order.

With layout analysis:
  detect regions → recognise each → reassemble ✓
  and you learn what's a table, a heading, a footer

means: Per-character or per-word certainty from the engine. It's the routing signal for what needs human review.
example: Fields below 80% confidence go to a review queue; above 95% auto-approve. That single rule cut manual review volume by 70%.
diagram:
word "₹4,500" conf 0.42  → review queue
word "Invoice" conf 0.99  → accept

Route by confidence, don't treat all output equally
how:
OCR engines don't return text — they return text plus, for each word or character, a number expressing how certain the engine was.

Most pipelines discard that number, which throws away the most operationally useful signal in the whole system. Confidence is what lets you treat a clean typed invoice differently from a crumpled fax, automatically, without a human looking at either.

The pattern is threshold routing. Above a high threshold, accept automatically. Below a low one, send to human review. In between, apply validation rules — does the total match the line items, is the date plausible, does the invoice number match the expected format.

That single mechanism is usually what makes a document pipeline economically viable, because it concentrates human attention on the small fraction that needs it.
more: Set thresholds per field rather than per document, because their stakes differ. A misread supplier name is an inconvenience; a misread payment amount is a financial error. And calibrate against your own ground truth set — engine confidence values are not comparable across engines or even across versions, so an inherited threshold means nothing.
diagram2:
Per field, not per document:

  invoice_number  0.97  → auto-accept
  supplier_name   0.88  → accept, low stakes
  total_amount    0.71  → REVIEW, high stakes
  due_date        0.94  → validate format, accept

Typical outcome:
  85% auto-processed
  15% reviewed by a human
  → the economics of the whole pipeline

Calibrate thresholds on YOUR ground truth.

means: Processing pages independently to keep tail latency sane, then reassembling. The main scaling lever in document pipelines.
example: A 400-page PDF processed serially takes 9 minutes and blocks the queue. Fanned out across 20 workers, it finishes in 30 seconds.
diagram:
400-page PDF
  ↓ split into page jobs
  ↓ 20 workers in parallel
  ↓ reassemble by page number
9 min → 30 sec

Track partial failure per page, not per document
how:
Document processing is slow per page, and page count varies enormously — one invoice, or a four-hundred-page filing.

Processing serially means a single large document occupies a worker for minutes. Everything queued behind it waits, including hundreds of one-page documents that would each take under a second. That's head-of-line blocking, and it shows up as wildly unpredictable latency for users whose documents are small.

Because pages are independent for recognition, the fix is straightforward: split into per-page jobs, fan them out across workers, and reassemble by page number.

The step people miss is tracking failure per page rather than per document. One page that won't parse should not discard the other three hundred and ninety-nine that processed fine.
more: Some operations genuinely can't be parallelised — tables continuing across pages, or documents whose classification depends on the whole. Handle those in a reassembly pass after per-page work completes, rather than forcing the whole document through a serial path for the sake of the few operations that need it.
diagram2:
SERIAL
  [400-page filing ████████████ 9 min]
  [1pg][1pg][1pg]  ← all waiting behind it ✗

PARALLEL
  split into 400 page jobs
  → 20 workers → reassemble by page number
  → 30 seconds ✓

Track failure PER PAGE:
  page 187 fails → 399 pages still succeed
  → partial result + one page flagged

Cross-page work (tables, classification)
happens in a reassembly pass.

means: Recovering rows and columns from a visual grid. Merged cells, spanning headers and borderless tables are where it breaks.
example: A borderless table with a merged header cell shifted every value one column left. Nothing errored; the numbers were just quietly wrong.
diagram:
Hard cases:
  ├ borderless tables
  ├ merged / spanning cells
  ├ multi-line cells
  └ tables split across pages

Always validate: column count, totals row
how:
A table is a visual convention. Humans read alignment and spacing as structure; a computer sees a scatter of text at coordinates and has to infer the grid.

Bordered tables are relatively easy — detect the lines, and the cells are defined. Everything else is inference from alignment, and that's where it breaks.

The dangerous failure is not an error. A merged header cell spanning two columns, or a borderless table where one column is slightly ragged, can shift every value one column to the left. Nothing throws. The output is a well-formed table of numbers in the wrong fields, and it looks entirely plausible downstream.

That's why table extraction needs validation rather than trust: column counts, totals that should reconcile, values that should match their expected type.
more: Tables spanning pages are their own problem: the header appears once, and rows on later pages arrive with no column context. Handling that requires stitching continuation rows to the original header, which the extractor won't do for you. It's worth testing explicitly, because multi-page tables are common in exactly the documents that matter — financial statements and long invoices.
diagram2:
Where it breaks:
  ├ no borders — structure inferred from alignment
  ├ merged / spanning header cells
  ├ multi-line cells (is that a new row?)
  └ tables continuing across pages

The dangerous case:
  a merged header shifts every value one column left
  → no error, plausible-looking numbers, all wrong ✗

Always validate:
  expected column count · totals reconcile
  types per column · page-continuation stitching
